prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The first three frames show a stable layered layout: very near foreground forms along the bottom edge (roughly 0.3–1 m), the pool table centered ahead (about 1–3 m), and darker furniture and room structure farther away (approximately 3–6+ m). The foreground forms partly occlude the lower pool table, while the table lies below the more distant background; repeated depth patterns suggest little approach or retreat before the camera turns right in frames 4–5. During that turn, the table and nearby foreground shift left and mostly leave view, exposing the right side of the room, but motion blur weakens object boundaries and prevents reliable person-facing or gaze estimates. The map makes near/middle/far layering clearer than RGB alone, but its brightness has no metric scale and the bright ceiling-like region in the last frames appears geometrically unreliable, so metre estimates are only rough.
descriptions.segmentation: In the first three frames, the map places several coloured instances mainly on the left and lower foreground, including large masks roughly 0.5–2 m from the wearer and small isolated masks farther ahead around 2–5 m; these indicate overlap and partial clipping at the bottom edge. The large upper-left and upper-middle masks sit above the lower foreground masks, while small masks near the centre-right are separated from them by several metres in image-derived scene depth; across frames 1–3, corresponding regions shift laterally with little clear depth change. Frames 4–5 contain almost no useful segmentation as the camera turns right, so objects leaving leftward and newly revealed objects cannot be tracked reliably. Instance colouring helps separate overlapping regions that are ambiguous in RGB, but labels such as “umbrella” and several “person” masks visibly disagree with the pool-table scene, and the map cannot reliably establish facing direction, gaze, arm’s reach, or inter-person distance.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it provides no detected body or hand joints and supports no direct estimate of posture, facing direction, gaze, interpersonal spacing, or reach. It also cannot distinguish whether any body is behind another object, partly outside the frame, approaching, retreating, or turning as the camera pans right. Relative to RGB, it adds no spatial information; its only spatially relevant result is that no skeleton was localized anywhere in the strip. This absence is unreliable as evidence that no people or hands are present, especially because the RGB is wide-angle, partly occluded, and strongly motion-blurred in the final two frames.
